DECISION AND OPINION ON REVIEW 
Timely Petition for Review under §19(b) of the Act having been filed by the Respondent 
and Petitioner herein and notice given to all parties, the Commission, after considering the issues 
of the reasonableness of the medical treatment, temporary total disability (“TTD”), and penalties 
and attorney fees, and being advised of the facts and law, modifies the Decision of the Arbitrator 
as stated below and otherwise affirms and adopts the Decision of the Arbitrator, which is attached 
hereto and made a part hereof. The Commission further remands this case to the Arbitrator for 
further proceedings for a determination of a further amount of temporary total compensation or of 
compensation for permanent disability, if any, pursuant to Thomas v. Industrial Commission, 78 
Ill.2d 327, 399 N.E.2d 1322, 35 Ill.Dec. 794 (1980). 
The Commission modifies the award of penalties pursuant to Section 19(l) of the Act and 
vacates the award of penalties and attorney fees pursuant to Sections 19(k) and 16 of the Act. 
Section 19(l) provides: 
If the employee has made written demand for payment of benefits 
under Section 8(a) or Section 8(b), the employer shall have 14 days 
after receipt of the demand to set forth in writing the reason for the

delay . . . In case the employer or his or her insurance carrier shall 
without good and just cause fail, neglect, refuse, or unreasonably 
delay the payment of benefits under Section 8(a) or Section 8(b), the 
Arbitrator or the Commission shall allow to the employee additional 
compensation in the sum of $30 per day for each day that the 
benefits under Section 8(a) or Section 8(b) have been so withheld or 
refused, not to exceed $10,000. A delay in payment of 14 days or 
more shall create a rebuttable presumption of unreasonable delay. 
Penalties under Section 19(l) are in the nature of a late fee. Mechanical Devices v. 
Industrial Comm’n, 344 Ill. App. 3d 752, 763, 800 N.E.2d 819, 828, 279 Ill. Dec. 531 (2003). In 
addition, the assessment of a penalty under Section 19(l) is mandatory “[i]f the payment is late, for 
whatever reason, and the employer or its carrier cannot show an adequate justification for the 
delay.” McMahan v. Industrial Comm’n, 183 Ill. 2d 499, 515, 702 N.E.2d 545, 552, 234 Ill. Dec. 
205 (1998). The standard for determining whether an employer has good and just cause for a delay 
in payment is defined in terms of reasonableness. Mechanical Devices, 344 Ill. App. 3d at 763, 
800 N.E.2d at 829. The employer has the burden of justifying the delay, and the employer’s 
justification for the delay is sufficient only if a reasonable person in the employer’s position would 
have believed that the delay was justified. Board of Education of the City of Chicago v. Industrial 
Comm’n, 93 Ill. 2d 1, 9-10, 442 N.E.2d 861, 865, 66 Ill. Dec. 300 (1982). The Commission’s 
evaluation of the reasonableness of the employer’s delay is a question of fact that will not be 
disturbed unless it is contrary to the manifest weight of the evidence. Crockett v. Industrial 
Comm’n, 218 Ill. App. 3d 116, 121-122, 578 N.E.2d 140, 143, 161 Ill. Dec. 13 (1991). 
While the Arbitrator awarded 19(l) penalties for the Respondent’s failure to pay TTD 
benefits, the decision did not address the issue of unpaid medical expenses. The record established 
that Petitioner introduced Exhibit 3, documenting outstanding medical bills from Northwestern 
totaling $3,384.00, and requested payment of these expenses. The evidence demonstrated that 
these medical bills have remained unpaid since at least June 8, 2019. 
The Respondent offered no written justification for this delay as required by the Act. The 
Respondent asserted at arbitration that the medical bills had been paid but presented no evidence 
to substantiate this claim and failed to address the issue in its Brief.  
As Respondent failed to offer an adequate justification for its delay, penalties are warranted 
for the nonpayment of the medical expenses, in addition to the nonpayment of the TTD benefits. 
Based on the duration of nonpayment, the statutory maximum penalty of $10,000.00 pursuant to 
Section 19(l) is assessed against the Respondent. 
Next, the Commission vacates the award of penalties and attorney fees under Sections 
19(k) and 16.

Section 19(k) provides, in pertinent part: “In case where there has been any unreasonable 
or vexatious delay of payment or intentional underpayment of compensation *** then the 
Commission may award compensation additional to that otherwise payable under the Act equal to 
50% of the amount payable at the time of such award.” Section 16 provides for an award of 
attorney fees when an award of additional compensation under Section 19(k) is appropriate. “The 
amount of [attorney] fees to be assessed is a matter committed to the discretion of the 
Commission.” Williams v. Industrial Comm’n, 336 Ill. App. 3d 513, 516, 784 N.E.2d 396, 399, 
271 Ill. Dec. 178 (2003). 
The standard for awarding penalties and attorney fees under Sections 19(k) and 16 is higher 
than the standard for awarding penalties under Section 19(l) because Sections 19(k) and 16 require 
more than an “unreasonable delay” in payment of an award. McMahan, 183 Ill 2d at 514-15, 702 
N.E.2d at 545. It is not enough for the claimant to show that the employer simply failed, neglected, 
or refused to make payment or unreasonably delayed payment without good and just 
cause. McMahan, 183 Ill. 2d at 515, 702 N.E.2d at 552. Instead, Section 19(k) penalties and 
Section 16 fees are “intended to address situations where there is not only a delay, but the delay is 
deliberate or the result of bad faith or improper purpose.” McMahan, 183 Ill. 2d at 515, 702 N.E.2d 
at 553. In addition, while Section 19(l) penalties are mandatory, the imposition of penalties and 
attorney fees under Section 19(k) and Section 16 fees is discretionary. Id. 
Petitioner claims entitlement to an additional award under Sections 19(k) and 16 for the 
outstanding workers’ compensation benefits. However, the Commission finds that Petitioner has 
not met the higher standard required under Section 19(k) (and in turn Section 16). While the 
Respondent’s nonpayment of the medical expenses and TTD benefits meets the standard of 
unreasonableness for 19(l) purposes, Respondent’s overall conduct, including its consistent 
payment of other medical expenses and its payment of TTD benefits and associated advances, 
militates against the imposition of penalties and fees under Section 19(k) and Section 16. In this 
regard, Petitioner failed to show that the delay in the payment of benefits was deliberate or the 
result of bad faith or improper purpose on the part of the Respondent. 
Finally, the Commission denies Petitioner’s request for maintenance benefits from 
November 1, 2024 through May 9, 2025. 
Section 8(a) of the Act provides that an employer “shall also pay for treatment, instruction 
and training necessary for the physical, mental and vocational rehabilitation of the employee, 
including all maintenance costs and expenses incidental thereto.” Because maintenance is awarded 
incidental to vocational rehabilitation, an employer is obligated to pay maintenance only “while 
[an employee] is engaged in a prescribed vocational-rehabilitation program.” Euclid Beverage v. 
Illinois Workers’ Compensation Comm’n, 2019 IL App (2d) 180090WC, (quoting W.B. Olson, 
Inc. v. Illinois Workers’ Compensation Comm’n, 2012 IL App (1st) 113129WC, ¶ 39, 981 N.E.2d 
25, 366 Ill. Dec. 960). “A claimant is generally entitled to vocational rehabilitation when he 
sustains a work-related injury which causes a reduction in his earning power and there is evidence 
that rehabilitation will increase his earning capacity.” Greaney v. Industrial Comm’n, 358 Ill. App. 
26IWCC0142

3d 1002, 1019, 832 N.E.2d 331, 295 Ill. Dec. 180 (2005). Vocational rehabilitation may include, 
but is not limited to, counseling for job searches, supervising job search programs, and vocational 
retraining, which includes education at an accredited learning institution. See 820 ILCS 305/8(a). 
An employee’s self-directed job search or vocational training may constitute a vocational-
rehabilitative program. Roper Contracting v. Industrial Comm’n, 349 Ill. App. 3d 500, 506, 812 
N.E.2d 65, 285 Ill. Dec. 476 (2004). 
In this case, Petitioner received permanent restrictions on October 31, 2024. However, 
there is no evidence that he requested, or was thereafter enrolled in, a vocational rehabilitation 
program. There is also no evidence that Petitioner engaged in a self-directed job search. 
Accordingly, the request for maintenance benefits is denied. 
All else is affirmed. 
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Decision of the 
Arbitrator filed July 17, 2025 is modified as stated above and otherwise affirmed and adopted.  
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Respondent shall pay to the 
Petitioner the sum of $1313.54 per week for a period of 281-6/7 weeks, June 8, 2019 through 
October 31, 2024, that being the period of temporary total incapacity for work under §8(b), and 
that as provided in §19(b) of the Act, this award in no instance shall be a bar to a further hearing 
and determination of a further amount of temporary total compensation or of compensation for 
permanent disability, if any. 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Respondent shall pay for the 
outstanding medical expenses from Northwestern Medicine, if not already paid, pursuant to 
Sections 8(a) and 8.2 of the Act.  
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Respondent shall pay to 
Petitioner penalties pursuant to Section 19(l) of the Act in the amount of $10,000.00. The 
Arbitrator’s award of penalties pursuant to Section 19(k) and Section 16 is hereby vacated.  
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Petitioner is entitled to a 
vocational assessment, pursuant to Section 8(a) of the Act and 50 Ill. Admin. Code Section 
9110.10.  
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that this case be remanded to the 
Arbitrator for further proceedings consistent with this Decision, but only after the latter of 
expiration of the time for filing a written request for Summons to the Circuit Court has expired 
without the filing of such a written request, or after the time of completion of any judicial 
proceedings, if such a written request has been filed.

DISSENT 
I respectfully dissent from that portion of the Majority’s decision vacating section 19(k) 
penalties and section 16 attorney fees. I would have increased the amount of each. The respondent 
had no legitimate basis to deny payment of medical expenses and/or TTD benefits. It’s been the 
law in the state of Illinois for over 40 years that failing to pay benefits because the petitioner suffers 
from non-work-related health conditions is improper. Bd. of Education v. Indus. Comm’n, 93 Ill. 
2d 20 (1982). The respondent admits that it failed to pay the benefits because of petitioner’s 
unrelated health conditions. The Majority asserts that respondent’s denials were not unreasonable 
or vexatious because it paid some medical expenses and TTD. The fact that respondent paid some 
benefits is simply not relevant, in my opinion, when the reason for not paying others violates 40 
years of precedent. Ignoring 40 years of precedent certainly seems unreasonable and vexatious to 
me. Therefore, I respectfully dissent.

FINDINGS 
 
On the date of accident, June 8, 2019, Respondent was operating under and subject to the provisions of the 
Act.   
 
On this date, an employee-employer relationship did exist between Petitioner and Respondent.   
 
On this date, Petitioner did sustain an accident that arose out of and in the course of employment.

services.

MEMORANDUM OF DECISION OF ARBITRATOR – 19(b) 
 
I. 
PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
 
Mr. Rory Gillett (“Petitioner”), by and through his attorney, filed an Application of Adjustment 
of Claim for benefits under the Workers’ Compensation Act (“Act”). 820 ILCS 305/1 et seq. (West 
2014). Petitioner alleged that he sustained an accidental injury on June 8, 2019 while employed 
by Kobotech, Inc. (“Respondent”). A hearing was held on May 9, 2025 on the following issues: 
causation, medical bills, prospective medical care, temporary total disability, penalties and fees, 
and vocational rehabilitation. 
 
Petitioner testified in support of his claim. Respondent submitted four (4) reports prepared by Dr. 
Aaron Bare, Section 12 examiner. (RX 1-4) The parties requested a written decision, including 
findings of fact and conclusions of law pursuant to the Act. (AX 1)  
 
II. 
FINDINGS OF FACT 
 
Petitioner’s Testimony -Regarding Job Duties and Accident 
 
Petitioner testified that he worked as a theatrical stage employee for almost thirty (30) years, since 
1996 as a member of the Local 2, International Theatrical Stage Employees (“IATSE”). (T. 10-
11) As a stagehand with Local 2, Petitioner stated that he does high steel rigging, carpentry to 
build the decks and stages anywhere in the city. (T. 11) He explained that high steel rigging 
involved pulling up the motors that pull up the lights, curtains, etc. (T. 11) He testified that he 
worked in the United Center, all the theaters including Broadway in Chicago, Auditorium Theatre, 
Opera House, and Allstate Arena. (T. 11)  
 
Petitioner further explained that as a high steel rigger, he usually walks out on the beams with a 
safety harness to hook the motors into the steel, wrap the steel around the beam, and put burlap

so that the steel does not bend on the beam. (T. 13-14) Petitioner testified that he and two (2) 
other employees pull the motors using ropes that weigh one to two tons which holds lights, stage, 
sound, and curtains. (T. 15)  
 
Petitioner testified that he has worked at Lollapalooza building stages. (T. 16) He explained that 
the steel comes in a crane – the guys on the bottom pin the steel, he climbs the truss to undo the 
crane, he climbs back down, they put up the I-beams to get the other truss and then the roof. (T. 
16-17) The weight of the equipment they use are “no less than 2 [to] 300 pounds.” (T. 17) 
Petitioner stated that he must physically be able to carry over 100 pounds. (T. 17)  
 
Petitioner testified that prior to June 8, 2019, he did not have any issues or problems or seek 
treatment for his left shoulder, he had not had any MRI or x-rays for his left shoulder, or have a 
recommendation for surgery for his left shoulder. (T. 17-18) Petitioner testified that prior to June 
8, 2019, he did have an MRI and x-rays for his left knee. (T. 18)  
 
Petitioner testified that on June 8, 2019, he was hired to work on the Pritzker Pavilion for the 
outdoor Blues Festival. (T. 18) He explained that after they set up the stage, he was loading and 
unloading the bands’ equipment from the trucks onto the stage that included lights, sound, and 
band gear such as a piano, amps, keyboards, and guitars. (T. 19) Petitioner testified that he was 
working with a co-worker, Dave Cooper, when he popped his shoulder out of socket. (T. 19) He 
explained that he was carrying the guitar player’s sound equipment off the stage, he walked down 
the ladder to hand off an equipment to a guy in a truck, and his left shoulder popped. (T. 20) He 
explained that there was a nurse who had him sit down because he started sweating and two (2) 
security guards carried him into an ambulance that took him to the Northwestern Hospital 
Emergency Room (“NW ER”). (T. 20) 
 
Petitioner’s Testimony – Regarding Medical Treatment 
 
Petitioner testified that he was evaluated at the NW ER and was told that he had dislocated his 
shoulder. (T. 20-21) They were able to pop it back in and Petitioner was discharged with a sling, 
a note to be off work, and to follow up with Northwestern Orthopaedic Surgery (“NWOS”). (T. 
21)  
 
Petitioner testified that on June 19, 2019, he followed up with NWOS and underwent x-rays and 
was recommended for an MRI. (T. 21) 
 
Petitioner testified that on June 20, 2019, he underwent an MRI that showed a rotator cuff tear 
and a labral tear. (T. 21-22) Petitioner testified on August 16, 2019, he had a surgery at the 
Northwestern Hospital (“NWH”). (T. 22) Petitioner claimed that he did not have any issues or 
complications from the surgery and remained in the hospital overnight due to his breathing issue. 
(T. 22-23)  
 
Petitioner testified that he had a follow up with NWOS on August 27, 2019 to have his stitches 
removed. (T. 23) He was told no lifting with his left arm and to return on October 1, 2019. (T. 24) 
Petitioner testified that he was evaluated on October 1, 2019 and was told to start physical therapy

with no lifting greater than five (5) pounds. (T. 24) Petitioner testified that he started physical 
therapy with Athletico. (T. 24-25) 
 
Petitioner testified that he returned to NWOS on November 12, 2019 and was instructed to 
continue with physical therapy and that they may proceed with a cortisone injection if problems 
persist. (T. 25)  
 
Petitioner testified that he next had an appointment at NWOS on December 2, 2019 and was 
instructed to continue with physical therapy and off work. (T. 25-26) Petitioner confirmed that 
his last physical therapy was on December 30, 2019. (T. 26) A Functional Capacity Evaluation 
(“FCE”) was completed in December of 2019 that indicated that Petitioner could not return to 
work as a stagehand. (T. 26)  
 
Petitioner testified that he had a follow up at NWOS on February 13, 2020 and was recommended 
to continue physical therapy, placed on light duty restrictions, and no lifting greater than twenty 
(20) pounds. (T. 26) During this visit, Petitioner explained that his physical therapist was present 
to answer any questions that the doctor had regarding his progress. (T. 26-27) Petitioner testified 
that his last physical therapy session was on February 14, 2020 and no additional sessions were 
authorized. (T. 27)  
 
Petitioner confirmed that on February 17, 2020, his therapist requested additional sessions but the 
insurance company had denied it. (T. 28)  
 
Petitioner testified that Respondent scheduled an IME exam with Dr. Aaron Bare on May 8, 2020 
and he recommended him to continue with physical therapy and placed him on no lifting greater 
than twenty (20) pounds. (T. 29) Petitioner confirmed that Respondent did not accommodate these 
restrictions set by Dr. Bare. (T. 29) Petitioner testified that physical therapy was not approved. 
(T. 29)  
 
Petitioner testified that he returned to see Dr. Vehniah Kristin Tjong on August 26, 2020 at NWOS 
for an evaluation. (T. 29-30) He was recommended to continue with physical therapy for strength 
and to return when completed. (T. 30) Petitioner testified that physical therapy was not approved. 
(T. 30) 
 
Petitioner testified that he returned to see Dr. Tjong on January 28, 2021 for an evaluation. (T. 
30) Petitioner confirmed that he told Dr. Tjong that physical therapy had not been approved and 
that he was doing a home exercise program. (T. 30) Petitioner explained that they had him buy a 
pulley which he set it up in his basement – he did pulley and light lifting and curls, in addition to 
stretching. (T. 31) Dr. Tjong again recommended physical therapy. (T. 31) Petitioner testified that 
on February 8, 2021, physical therapy was finally reinstated. (T. 31)  
 
Petitioner testified that on April 15, 2021, he attended another IME session with Dr. Bare. (T. 32) 
Petitioner confirmed that Dr. Bare recommended him to continue with physical therapy and no 
lifting greater than ten (10) pounds overhead. (T. 32-33)

Petitioner testified that physical therapy was again reinstated on May 7, 2021. (T. 33) Petitioner

Petitioner testified that on August 26, 2021, he called his doctor’s office to request his

was terminated. (T. 33) Petitioner identified PX 2 as a document from the insurance company 
dated August 26, 2021 at 8:44 am indicating that they would not authorize any more physical

Petitioner testified that his appointment was moved up and he was able to follow up with Dr. 
Tjong on September 8, 2021. (T. 34) Dr. Tjong recommended Petitioner to continue with physical 
therapy. (T. 34) Petitioner confirmed that Dr. Tjong instructed him to return to work on light duty 
and to return to see her in three (3) months. (T. 34-35) Petitioner testified that there was “no such 
thing as light duty as a stagehand.” (T. 35) Petitioner testified that Respondent did not 
accommodate his light duty restrictions. (T. 35)  
 
Petitioner testified that he followed up with Dr. Tjong on January 20, 2022 and Dr. Tjong noted 
that Petitioner was battling with workers’ compensation regarding physical therapy. (T. 35)  
 
Petitioner testified that Respondent sent him to meet with Dr. Bare on January 19, 2022. (T. 35-
36) He had another follow up with Dr. Bare on March 7, 2022 and was recommended for an 
arthrogram and placed on no return to work with 20-pound lifting restriction. (T. 36) Petitioner 
confirmed physical therapy and arthrogram was not approved and his temporary total benefits 
were terminated on March 1, 2023. (T. 36)  
 
Petitioner testified that he followed up with Dr. Tjong on March 1, 2023. (T. 36) He confirmed 
that Dr. Tjong noted that he had some issues with his heart and had a heart ablation. (T. 36-37) 
Petitioner believed he “went from 100 miles an hour to zero” “working every day, pulling up 
motors, and then nothing because the shoulder is out.” (T. 37) He testified he had more than two 
cardiac ablations on outpatient basis. (T. 37) Petitioner stated that he did not participate in any 
cardiac rehab. (T. 37) Dr. Tjong recommended physical therapy to continue. (T. 38) Petitioner 
confirmed that on January 9, 2024, physical therapy was approved and he began his sessions on 
January 10, 2024 to March of 2024, nineteen (19) sessions total. (T. 38) The therapist noted that 
Petitioner had not met his goal for lifting to return to work. (T. 38-39) Petitioner testified a request 
was made for additional physical therapy that was denied. (T. 39) 
 
Petitioner testified that he saw Dr. Tjong on October 31, 2024. (T. 39) Dr. Tjong noted that 
additional physical therapy was denied and Petitioner was doing a home exercise program. (T. 
39-40) Petitioner explained that he does stretching wheel and lifting with 5-pound dumbbells. (T. 
40) He confirmed that Dr. Tjong placed him on no lifting overhead and no lifting greater than 8-

Decisions of an arbitrator shall be based exclusively on the evidence in the record of the 
proceeding and material that has been officially noticed.  820 ILCS 305/1.1(e).  Credibility is the 
quality of a witness which renders his evidence worthy of belief.  The Arbitrator, whose province 
it is to evaluate witness credibility, evaluates the demeanor of the witness and any external 
inconsistencies with his/her testimony.  Where a claimant’s testimony is inconsistent with his/her 
actual behavior and conduct, the Commission has held that an award cannot stand. McDonald v. 
Industrial Commission, 39 Ill. 2d 396 (1968); Swift v. Industrial Commission, 52 Ill. 2d 490 
(1972).   
 
It is the function of the Commission to judge the credibility of the witnesses and to resolve 
conflicts in the medical evidence and assign weight to witness testimony. O’Dette v. Industrial 
Commission, 79 Ill.2d 249, 253, 403 N.E.2d 221, 223 (1980); Hosteny v. Workers’ Compensation 
Commission, 397 Ill. App. 3d 665, 674 (2009).  Internal inconsistencies in a claimant’s testimony, 
as well as conflicts between the claimant’s testimony and medical records, may be taken to 
indicate unreliability. Gilbert v. Martin & Bayley/Hucks, 08 ILWC 004187 (2010).

Issue F, whether Petitioner’s current condition of ill-being is causally related to the injury, the 
Arbitrator finds as follows:  
 
The Arbitrator adopts her findings of fact and conclusions of law contained above and incorporates

 To obtain compensation under the Act, a claimant must prove that some act or phase of his 
employment was a causative factor in his ensuing injuries.  A work-related injury need not be the 
sole or principal causative factor, as long as it was a causative factor in the resulting condition of 
ill-being.  Even if the claimant had a preexisting degenerative condition which made him more 
vulnerable to injury, recovery for an accidental injury will not be denied as long as he can show 
that his employment was also a causative factor. Thus, a claimant may establish a causal 
connection in such cases if he can show that a work-related injury played a role in aggravating his 
preexisting condition. Sisbro, Inc. v. Industrial Comm'n, 207 Ill. 2d 193, 205, 797 N.E.2d 665, 278 
Ill. Dec. 70 (2003). “A chain of events which demonstrates a previous condition of good health, 
an accident, and a subsequent injury resulting in disability may be sufficient circumstantial 
evidence to prove a causal nexus between the accident and the employee’s injury.” International 
Harvester v. Industrial Com., 93 Ill. 2d 59, 63 442 N.E.2d 908 (1982). 
 
In this case, Respondent does not dispute that Petitioner suffered an accident arising out of and in 
the course of his employment. However, Respondent disputes Petitioner’s current medical issues 
are causally related to said accident. Respondent points to a work status report dated September 
17, 2021 by PA Bradley Pennington that stated that his cardiologist believes his current cardiac 
condition may ultimately prevent him from ever returning to full-duty work. (PX 1 p. 466)  
 
Additionally, Respondent points to Petitioner’s treating surgeon, Dr. Tjong, dated January 20, 
2022, where she added that Petitioner’s current inability to return to work is primarily due to 
serious, non-work-related cardiac conditions rather than the accepted left shoulder injury. (PX 1 
pp. 442-454) She further added that there had been delay in physical therapy approval for the 
shoulder and recent medical development showed that Petitioner now suffered from prolonged A-
fib and congestive heart failure. (PX 1 p. 444) 
 
Finally, Respondent points to Dr. Tjong’s notes from March 1, 2023. (PX 1 pp. 401-412) Dr. 
Tjong reported that since the surgery, Petitioner had developed multiple serious medical 
conditions – including two (2) cardiac ablations, kidney failure, liver damages from medications 
and thyroid issues – which have prevented him from doing home exercises. (PX 1 pp. 404) She 
further noted that Petitioner’s cardiac condition was now stable, there was no concern for a retear 
of the rotator cuff, and he had been advised to resume physical therapy for strength and range of 
motion. (PX 1 p. 404) 
 
Upon careful review of Petitioner’s testimony and medical records, the Arbitrator disagrees with 
Respondent’s position for the following reasons:

Second, the letter written by PA Bradley Pennington states the following: “Mr. Rory Gillett is a

For all the reasons stated above, the Arbitrator finds that Petitioner has proven by a preponderance 
of evidence that his current condition of ill-being with respect to his left shoulder is causally related

With regards to Section 19(1), the Act reads, 
 
In case the employer or his or her insurance carrier shall without good and just 
cause fail, neglect, refuse, or unreasonably delay the payment of benefits under 
Section 8(a) or Section 8(b), the Arbitrator or the Commission shall allow to the 
employee additional compensation in the sum of $ 30 per day for each day that the 
benefits under Section 8(a) or Section 8(b) have been so withheld or refused, not to 
exceed $ 10,000. A delay in payment of 14 days or more shall create a rebuttable 
presumption of unreasonable delay. 
 
820 ILCS 305/19(1) 
 
Case law dictates that penalties authorized by Section 19(1) serve as a late fee and apply whenever 
the employer or its carrier simply fails or neglects to make payment or unreasonably delays 
payment "without good and just cause." McMahan v. Industrial Comm'n, 702 N.E.2d 545 at 553 
(1998). If the payment is late, for whatever reason, and the employer or its carrier cannot show an 
adequate justification for the delay, an award of Section 19(1) penalties is mandatory. Id (emphasis 
added).

The standard for determining whether an employer has good and just cause for a delay in payment 
is defined in terms of reasonableness. Board of Education of the City of Chicago v. Industrial 
Comm'n, 442 N.E.2d 861 at 865 (1982). The employer has the burden of justifying the 
delay. Id. The employer's justification for the delay is sufficient only if a reasonable person in the 
employer's position would have believed that the delay was justified. Id. 
 
Petitioner is seeking temporary total disability from June 8, 2019 through May 9, 2025, the date 
of the hearing. Petitioner testified that his temporary total disability was not paid from February 1, 
2023 to April 20, 2023, from June 27, 2023 to July 31, 2023, and terminated on July 15, 2024. 
Respondent states that because there is significant treatment gaps related to the left shoulder and 
at times, Petitioner was not actively treating for his left shoulder, he is not entitled to temporary 
total disability for the entire period from June 8, 2019 through May 9, 2025. Respondent has not 
presented any cause, let along a good cause, why temporary total disability should not be paid 
through October 31, 2024, the date he was found to be at MMI by treating surgeon, Dr. Tjong. 
Respondent’s IME, Dr. Bare never found him at MMI at any point. The Arbitrator again notes that 
Petitioner testified to a new IME exam with Dr. Bare on March 31, 2025 but a report from that 
exam was not introduced and therefor, not admitted into evidence.  
 
As the Arbitrator finds that Respondent was unable to show an adequate justification for its delay, 
an award of Section 19(1) penalties is mandatory. The Arbitrator fines Respondent $30.00 a day 
starting February 1, 2023 through April 20, 2023, June 27, 2023 through July 31, 2023, and July 
15, 2024 through October 31, 2024, a total of 229 days. $30.00 per day multiplied by 229 days 
equals $6,870.00. Therefore, the Arbitrator imposes penalties of $6,870.00 under Section 19(1) 
against Respondent, to be paid directly to Petitioner. 
 
Section 19(k) Penalties 
 
The Act reads, 
 
In cases where there has been any unreasonable or vexatious delay of payment or 
intentional underpayment of compensation, or proceedings have been instituted or 
carried on by the one liable to pay the compensation, which do not present a real 
controversy, but are merely frivolous or for delay, then the Commission may award 
compensation additional to that otherwise payable under this Act equal to 50% of 
the amount payable at the time of such award. Failure to pay compensation in 
accordance with the provisions of Section 8, paragraph (b) of this Act, shall be 
considered unreasonable delay. When determining whether this subsection (k) shall 
apply, the Commission shall consider whether an Arbitrator has determined that the 
claim is not compensable or whether the employer has made payments under 
Section 8(j). 
 
820 ILCS 305/19(k). 
 
While Section 19(1) penalties apply when Respondent delays payment "without good and just 
cause," Section 19(k) penalties require a lack of good faith. The Commission has the discretion to 
impose Section 19(k) penalties where there is not only a delay in payment, but the delay was in

A claimant is generally entitled to vocational rehabilitation when he sustains a work-related injury 
which causes a reduction in his earning power and there is evidence that rehabilitation will 
increase his earning capacity. Euclid Bev. v. Illinois Workers' Compensation Comm'n, 2019 IL 
App (2d) 180090WC, ¶ 29, 124 N.E.3d 1027 citing Greaney v. Industrial Comm'n, 358 Ill. App. 
3d 1002, 1019, 832 N.E.2d 331, 295 Ill. Dec. 180 (2005). Because the primary goal of 
rehabilitation is to return the injured employee to work (Schoon v. Industrial Comm'n, 259 Ill. 
App. 3d 587, 594, 630 N.E.2d 1341, 197 Ill. Dec. 217 (1994)), if the injured employee has 
sufficient skills to obtain employment without further training or education, that factor weighs 
against an award of vocational rehabilitation. National Tea Co. v. Industrial Comm'n, 97 Ill. 2d 
424, 432, 454 N.E.2d 672, 73 Ill. Dec. 575 (1983). Moreover, an injured employee is generally 
not entitled to vocational rehabilitation if the evidence shows that he does not intend to return to 
work, although able to do so. Schoon, 259 Ill. App. 3d at 594. 
 
Petitioner is seeking vocational rehabilitation. However, this issue was not addressed in his 
proposal. On the other hand, Respondent states that because Petitioner failed to demonstrate a 
consistent or good faith effort to seek suitable employment, he is not entitled to vocational 
rehabilitation service.  
 
It is obvious from Petitioner and his wife’s testimony that he is unable to return to his previous 
employment as a stagehand. This is supported by the medical record that includes the IME reports. 
Based on this, the Arbitrator orders a vocational assessment, pursuant to Section 8(a) of the Act 
and 50 Ill.Admin. code Section 9110.10.
